We, the People of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic
contentEn: The un-lockdown is under way, and some privileged ones like us sit in our homes working and watching and reading day after day about the endless cruelty that is being heaped all around us. On migrant workers who walked miles and miles in their desperation to return home, on informal sector workers who have not had a decent meal to eat, and nowhere to call home. While we sink further into our misery, our thoughts move back and forth on all that has transpired in the last many months: what happened to all the anti CAA-NRC-NPR protestors hounded and threatened, their protest sites ripped apart? What happened to the victims of the violence that erupted in North East Delhi, largely Muslims, many of whom find themselves being arrested and jailed for the very violence that destroyed their lives? What new forms will the peaceful protests against the unjust CAA-NRC-NPR look like? In fact, will we ever see them take over the streets again? Do the whitewashed walls of Shaheen Bagh still hold our collective rage, and the imagination of our democratic nation? At times like these, looking back and reminiscing seems like an almost indecent luxury. Nevertheless, reflect and write we must, for the raging powerful light of Shaheen Baghs have shown us the way for eons to come. The light begins to change. Write, Write Down I am a Miya, My serial number in the NRC is 200543 I have two children Another is coming Next summer. Will you hate him, as you hate me? - Hafiz Ahmed, Miya poet, Assam  Darkness descends. “Pakistan’s Hindu community unanimously rejects this bill, which is tantamount to dividing India on communal lines,” said the Pakistan Hindu Council. Things get darker. Soon after CAA 2019 became the law of the land, many protests, dharnas, rallies, press conferences sprung up all over the country, and by the signs of it, the government wasn’t in a mood for any of that. After all, good, abiding citizens are just meant to buy (with our duly demonetised currency) every half-truth and full lie sold to us through parliamentary statements, sarkari slogans, ads, the godi media and every other weapon in the propaganda arsenal. But, the people, it seems, hadn’t got the script. Not just in the ‘legally designated’ protest spaces like Jantar Mantar in Delhi, Azad Maidan in Bombay, Vidhan Soudha in Bangalore, but also in college campuses, residential areas, on streets and in marketplaces, across the country, voices against CAA-NRC-NPR started getting louder. Uff, what a nuisance the subjects are being! Time to crack down on, and stem the tide. And what better place to start than at a fairly routine protest within the campus of the Jamia Millia Islamia (JMI) University in Delhi. Statements and thoughts against CAA-NRC-NPR International critiques/statements against CAA-NRC-NPR  Peoples’ Tribunal on Contested Citizenship, Assam Hearing the testimonies of those excluded from the final list of NRC and various leading experts, the jury comprising former SC judges Madan B Lokur and Kurian Joseph, former Delhi High Court Chief Justice AP Shah and Professor Faizan Mustafa, Vice Chancellor, Nalsar University of Law, Hyderabad, former Planning Commission member Syeda Hamid, Ambassador Deb Mukherjee, Githa Hariharan of Indian Writers’ Forum and Professor Monirul Hussain, said, ‘We all agree that the NRC has spawned a humanitarian crisis. We worry because there are no signs of this crisis abating. Large numbers of minorities in Assam, whether religious, linguistic or ethnic, have lived with the fear of being told that they don’t belong in this country. They may, at any time, be marked doubtful voters (or D-Voter) and prevented from exercising their franchise. A local border police constable can, again, at any time, accuse them of being foreigners and refer their cases to a detention centre. Even after the final register, there are many demands for selective reverification.’ Thanks for the interruption! Winds of change start wafting in from near the Yamuna.  The women of Shaheen Bagh, the dadis of Shaheen Bagh, the children of Shaheen Bagh occupied the main Kalindi Kunj road and started a peaceful sit-in with only one demand: ‘Take back CAA-NRC-NPR’. And soon, Shaheen Baghs were springing up all over the city – in Khureji Khas, Jama Masjid, Turkman Gate, Shahi Eidgah, Nizamuddin, Seelampur, Hauz Rani, Chand Bagh, Inderlok... 27 plus sites. And beyond Delhi there sprung, literally, hundreds of protests sites across Lucknow, Kolkata, Ranchi, Gaya, Kanpur, Hyderabad, Patna, Bangalore, Kolkata, Varanasi... in Europe, the US, Canada and so on.  As day became night, and nights blossomed into songs, slogans and chatter, these sites attracted to themselves many like us, battered and weary in our quest for ‘woh subah kabhi toh aayegi’. Spending whatever time we could with the women and students, soaking in the energy and doing our bit: talking to the women, volunteering at the medical counter, discovering new slogans, singing and performing, teaching and playing with the children at the Savitribai Phule and other libraries/ activity centres set up for the children at many of the sites, raising issues related to the CAA, religious and caste discrimination, the idea of the nation and much more. The idea of the Shaheen Baghs was like an eternal spring – a fresh, sparkling source of untiring energy for a community which has been targeted by lynchings, harassment and systematic political exclusion over the past several years, and whose defence mechanism has largely been to invisibilize itself in public. But let’s be honest, they were much more than the voice of the community, they were the voice we all had been seeking in our so-called ‘intersectional politics.’ Young and old women, many of them illiterate, who were soon effortlessly drawing their strength and articulation from, and teaching us a lesson or two about, the Constitution, Babasaheb Ambedkar, Fatima Sheikh, Savitribai Phule, Bhagat Singh, Ashfaqulla Khan, Ram Prasad Bismil, and Gandhi. After a very, very long time of hate, divisive and destructive politics, we saw a glimmer of democracy re-imagined, citizenship owned and asserted in ways so creative that they will forever be etched in our minds. As we stood/sat together reading the Preamble in multiple languages at India Gate, with Radhika Vemula and Saira Bano on Republic Day, singing the national anthem on New Year’s Eve with a sense of belief in its possibilities! What a miracle that was/is.  An image, an idea, that we have not seen evoked in movements since possibly the independence struggle, was the use of the Tricolour. The Flag was everywhere, held high. The National Anthem was sung daily at many sit-ins. As reading the Preamble became the norm at protests across the country, we the people, who believe, that we don’t need to wear our patriotism on our sleeve pivoted between cringing at this overt show of nationalism, and the awe we felt for those who reclaimed these symbols from the clutches of the right wing. Putting an end to any questions about their ‘Indian-ness’, perhaps. Making us think about our politics and privileges in completely new ways. Simultaneously, there were multiple protest events across the country. If so many hundreds of thousands marched to Azad Maidan in Mumbai, that the only way to see the whole crowd was from the top of a multi- storeyed building; coordinated national marches led by women, trans* and queer communities, students etc; and so many plays and skits and songs and verses and memes and online action... that all spoke to resisting the CAA-NRC-NPR package deal that is being thrust upon us. #Reject CAA #RejectNRC #Reject NPR As the popularity of these protests grew, the international attention began to be a problem for the State and its fellows. The government (both Delhi and Central) refused to meet the protestors and engage with their demands, despite the most loving missives from the protestors. Instead, right wing groups repeatedly attempted to ‘ukhaad nikaalo’ the protests, the state arbitrarily withdrew permissions given for protests, blocked metro stations to prevent people from reaching rally and protest sites, picked people up from the sites and took them on a Dilli-darshan for hours to try to stop them from protesting. Of course, we the (problematic) citizens would turn around and rejoin the protesting masses the moment they let us off in some obscure corner of the city. And thank heavens we did, because those were days we could still protest on the streets, remember?   But let’s face it, all the romance of the protests aside, things were getting a bit crazy. Take for example the trajectory of cases against these two 19 year olds: Ram Bhagat Gopal Sharma, shot at the protestors at JMI screaming ‘ye lo azaadi’, while the police stood around with folded arms and let a student get injured. Amulya Leona went onto the stage of an anti-CAA event in Bangalore organised by the All India Majlis-e-Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen (AIMIM ), and proclaimed ‘Long Live All Nations’... and among the nations she said ‘zindabad’ to was Pakistan. She was charged with sedition under the dreaded UAPA, while Sharma was out on bail within the week or so. Leona finally received bail only after spending 6 months in jail. Meanwhile, someone threw a petrol bomb at the protest site in Shaheen Bagh, the police did an unprovoked lathi charge at the Hauz Rani site, the story was turning... In the midst of it, came the Delhi elections, marked by just one thing: talk of governance by the AAP party, and hate speech against the Muslim community by the BJP and its allies. Deeply shocked by this, Saheli, along with 175 other feminist and human rights organisations and activists, issued an Open Letter to the Prime Minister on 3 February 2020, saying, ‘Vote for BJP or you will get raped? Is this your message to Delhi’s women? Your party is also exhorting mobs to aim bullets at women & children... Fight the election upholding the dignity of our Constitution.’   It's a night without end. A report titled, “The Role of Health Systems in Responding to Communal Violence” by the Jan Swasthya Abhiyan (JSA), speaks of the apathy with which victims of violence were treated at government hospitals, that is, if they managed to reach one because mobs continued to obstruct the movement of ambulances. At the hospitals themselves, there were several instances of patients not bring provided with adequate treatment, with one doctor even calling the victim a terrorist and extremist, and cruelly, bodies not being handed over to families for days on end. In a letter to Delhi CM Kejriwal, the JSA elaborated, “We have also been made aware of instances where hospitals are denying admission to injured persons whose MLCs were done in a different hospital, without the MLC number and treatment records. Families and patients are thus being penalized and harassed for not producing documents which are being denied to them in the first place... Hospitals are not proactively supporting families of injured people... families are running from pillar to post to identify their missing relatives. Multiple individuals who have been victims of violence have reported instances of being subjected to discriminatory language by staff members at hospitals. A few people have even expressed fear of going to government hospitals, instead choosing to access critical care at local clinics.” In the weeks that followed, Eidgah-Mustafabad became a relief camp site where about 1200 people took shelter, people whose homes were burnt, livelihood destroyed, and those who were too fearful of going back. The camp, of course, had no proper tenting, no toilets and nothing for people to eat. Add to that the relentless rains that lashed Delhi those days, soaking the mattresses and robbing victims of even their sleep. Several citizen initiatives sprang up in response to these terrible events: to offer rescue and refuge to victims; to offer medical aid and relief support; to remind government officials, agencies, bodies of their constitutional duty to protect all citizens; to reach out with food, clothing, sanitary products, rations and other essentials; to counsel and help the old and the young and the children in this time of trauma; to offer immediate aid to those disabled or paralyzed due to injuries. Peace committees were formed to reach out to at the neighbourhood level. Called ‘Aman ki Aawazein’, we went from one locality to another with messages of peace, justice, harmony and togetherness. A meal here, a song there, a poem read, a sharing of information of rights guaranteed by the courts... all sharing a moment in solidarity in times of duress. Excerpts from the first citizen’s report titled, ‘Let us heal our Dilli’ by Farah Naqvi, Sarojini N, Navsharan Singh, Naveen Chander. ‘The targeting of Muslims in North east Delhi reminded one distinctly of the targeting of Sikhs in Delhi in 1984 and of Muslims in Gujarat 2002. The targeted damage to property and means of livelihood for people who live on the edge of survival is truly vile. Thelas burnt, small shops burnt, autorickshaws burnt, e-rickshaws burnt, a scrap market burnt. These are means of livelihood for some of India’s poorest people.’ ‘In one case that we encountered, the attack on Hindu properties was by right-wing mobs themselves. An autorickshaw owner/driver, on the main road outside Gokulpuri flailed helplessly but angrily at the injustice of what happened to him – two of his autorickshaws which he proudly pointed out say ‘Jai Mata Di’ on the back, were burnt because in one of them he was ferrying Muslim passengers and the mob probably thought he was Muslim too. “I am a Hindu!” he kept saying.’ Even as the Covid-19 crisis became a global pandemic, the central government refused to take back its order to start updation of the NPR along with house listing for the Census 2021 from 1 April, 2020. So more than 1000 women from across 20 states of India, wrote to every state Chief Minister in the country saying, “NPR presents a clear danger to women, so we demand de-linking of NPR from census house listing.” Addressing a crowded press conference in Delhi, women rights activists, including Annie Raja, Farah Naqvi, Anjali Bhardwaj, Vani Subramanian, Meera Sanghamitra, Mariam Dhawle and Poonam Kaushik said, “Women constitute nearly 50% of India’s population, and all women, irrespective of caste and religious community will be affected by this regime that puts our citizenship to test in a totally arbitrary and frightening manner.” At the same time, the activists welcomes the fact that Kerala and West bengal had already issued stay orders on the roll out of the NPR. Maybe, this time, the light will break through. What happens next? Who knows. But it seems that the chasm between the haves, the ones who belong, whose citizenry is guaranteed; and all the rest, has become a painful putrid gash. This hurt was for all to see in the plight of migrant workers during lockdown. Thrown out of work, walking endlessly on foot, dying of hunger, dragging along their measly belongings and their broken hearts.  CONDEMNING CRACKDOWN ON WOMEN ACTIVISTS IN DELHI 1,100+ FEMINISTS ACROSS RELIGION, CLASS, CASTE, ETHNICITY, ABILITY, SEXUALITY AND GENDERS ISSUE SOLIDARITY STATEMENT 3 May, 2020: We, the undersigned, strongly condemn the brazenly malicious attacks, arrests and intimidation by the Delhi Police of Muslim women, students and activists, as well as other citizens who have spoken up against the unconstitutional moves of the present ruling dispensation. Media reports that about 800 + anti-CAA protesters have been detained or arrested since the Covid 19 lockdown, which means they have had little or no access to lawyers and legal aid, and their families given no information of their whereabouts for extended periods after they were in custody. The impunity with which the Delhi Police is carrying out this sweep under direct orders from the Home Ministry is facilitated by the reduced media, public and legal scrutiny under the lockdown. As feminists, we decry this systematic crackdown on, and mis-representation of, the peaceful and constitutional anti-CAA-NRC-NPR movement. Led so powerfully by Muslim women across the country, these protests witnessed a new wave of women stepping out in their own neighbourhoods in huge numbers, defying social structures and asserting their rights as citizens of a secular, democratic republic—one of the most historic moments and movements, since independence. In Delhi itself, from the Dadis of Shaheen Bagh to the spirited women from Jamia, Hauz Rani, Jama Masjid, Nizamuddin, Seelampur, etc, the women’s spectacular leadership and the solidarities they formed across communities and locations inspired millions across the world, but evidently, also shook the foundations of the ruling elite. After all, until these women organised themselves with such clarity, and commitment to democratic values, the only use the government had for them was as symbols of repression to be ‘saved’ from Muslim customary practices such as the Triple Talaq. GULFISHA, 25, is one such young muslim woman who emerged a leader in the Seelampur anti-CAA protest. An MBA student, Gulfisha has reportedly been arrested by the police on 9th April, but until this day, the details remain blurry. She has been languishing in judicial custody under false charges of sedition, without proper access to her family or lawyer. The Covid lockdown has brought jail mulakats to a standstill, and no alternative means of communication such as telephonic contact are available to be apprised of her state of health or well-being. The same holds for numerous men from Seelampur who were allegedly picked up by the police at about the same time as Gulfisha, although their exact whereabouts are not known. SAFOORA ZARGAR, 30, member of the Jamia Coordination Committee has been arrested despite being three months’ pregnant—at a time when overcrowding in prisons and have become a huge concern worldwide. Former Municipal Councillor, ISHRAT JAHAN, active in the Khureji protest has been in jail for over a month now, and been subjected to custodial torture. Her co-accused, Khalid Saifi emerged from police custody with both his legs as well as two fingers broken—indicating brutal torture. We have good reason to fear for the rights and safety of Gulfisha, Safoora, Ishrat and others like them: as women, as undertrial prisoners, and as those falsely charged under the draconian Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA). Some of the other student activists arrested and slapped with draconian charges and sent to judicial custody include Meeran Haider (President, RJD Youth Wing, Delhi), Sharjeel Imam (JNU scholar), Shifa-Ur-Rehman (President, Jamia Alumni Association). Dr. Umar Khalid of United Against Hate has also been reportedly slapped with UAPA and is ‘under investigation’. In an unprecedented and shameless move, the Delhi Police has now even booked Zafarul Islam Khan, Chairman, Delhi Minorities Commission under sedition charges! We must remember that inspired by Shaheen Bagh, sit-in protests led by Muslim women were held in 200+ locations across the country. Holding up images of Savitri Bai, Fatima Sheikh, Babasaheb Ambedkar, painting protest graffiti and reading the Preamble, reciting poetry and slogans upholding constitutional values and communal harmony, this was a tremendously powerful assertion of rights and resistance, of historically marginalized women creating the possibility of a new nation of emancipation, justice, equality and dignity. In response, the majoritarian forces of the Hindu right, shifted the register of contestation by unleashing multiple attacks on these gatherings, culminating in a pre-planned communal pogrom targeting the Muslims in North-East Delhi. The government, unwilling to dialogue with the women, chose the masculinist response of trying to crush them. Its message is clear—those who dare challenge its fascist, patriarchal, communal, classist and casteist nature will be meted the harshest State sanctions. Countless detentions, interrogation and intimidation of women and student activists from many anti-CAA protest sites and universities like Jamia, bear testimony to how brazenly the State is using everything, including the pandemic, to silence more than just one Gulfisha or Safoora; to warn all Muslim women who dare to speak out. For minority communities to exist in India today seems to be a provocation, for them to question and think seems to be a greater trouble, and of course, to protest and sing songs of azaadi is apparently just too much. Not surprisingly, a malicious and false narrative that ‘the peaceful protests by women were the cause of the violence in Delhi’ has been propagated by the police, fanned by sections of the media and vested interests to camouflage the explicit political nature of the violence, carried out with the collusion and participation of security forces. Despite claims by the police of ‘finding the real culprits’, the organized and premeditated nature of the violence on the minority community and the great asymmetry in losses and deaths between affected communities is yet to be accounted for. Right-wing leaders of the BJP such as Kapil Mishra and Anurag Thakur who openly threatened violence have not even been named in FIRs. Those who fired at gatherings are out on bail. Reports of ‘out-of-towners’ brought in to perpetuate the violence have yet to be subjects of investigation. After all of this, the community which bore the brunt of the communal violence most, including the peaceful women protesters and men, is being projected as the ‘aggressor’ and demeaned in numerous ways through vicious propaganda. Hundreds of Muslims are being picked up and incarcerated. There is no clarity on the total number of FIRs, arrests and detentions. Muslim women and other activists who worked with them in solidarity towards a shared concept of citizenship and feminist sisterhood are also being systematically vilified. Media reports that in the last some days, the police has seized the phones of AISA activist Kawalpreet Kaur and few activists of Pinjra Tod. Worrying accounts of women students who were active in the peaceful protests, being targeted are also coming to the fore. Taking cognizance of such ground realities, the Delhi High Court as recently as on 27th April, directed the Delhi Police to comply with the DK Basu guidelines regarding arrests and detentions. In the long run, these attacks by the State will affect far more than members of just one community. Much like the NRC project that is bound to deprive the poor and marginalized across religious groups of citizenship rights, the present focus on terrorizing Muslims instead of tackling the Covid-19 pandemic reveals a deep apathy towards safeguarding the lives and well-being of millions of toiling poor across the country, many of whom belong to the ‘majority’ community. We remember with hope and inspiration the vibrant anti-CAA protests across the country from December to February. We remember that while the State was firing tear gas shells in libraries and mercilessly lathi-charging peaceful protesters and students, while the police stood by as vigilante gunmen opened fire, these protesters stood strong and fearless in their determination against the Hindutva project. They are the conscience keepers of the nation, and we salute them! The actions of the State only reveal how much it fears such voices, and how far it will go to subvert the cause of truth and justice. We declare our unflinching solidarity with the Muslim women, students and activists who worked together as harbingers of peace and shall defeat sinister attempts to project them in bad light by the state and vested interests. We demand: To this oppressive regime, we say yet again: इस खुले झूठ को, जेहन की लूट को, मैं नहीं मानती, मैं नहीं जानती!  तोड़ तोड़ के बंधनो को देखो बहने आती हैं!  आएंगी ज़ुल्म िमटाएंगी, वो तो नया ज़माना लाएंगी!
contentHi: इस खुले झूठ को, जेहन की लूट को, मैं नहीं मानती, मैं नहीं जानती!  तोड़ तोड़ के बंधनो को देखो बहने आती हैं!  आएंगी ज़ुल्म िमटाएंगी, वो तो नया ज़माना लाएंगी!

titleEn: They don't make them like you anymore, Kalpana
contentEn:
Ilina Sen portrait This remembrance note must start with an apology to Kalpana Mehta. One day, when we were doing our usual adda-baazi she said, ‘Don’t try to write me off with a few pages of an obituary, I want a whole issue of the Saheli Newsletter on me.’ And Vani had replied flippantly, ‘Who’s going to put in so much effort, Kalpana? You’d better write it yourself, and translate it into Hindi as well, before you go.’ We all laughed out, our loud cackles filling the room, and hers crinkling up her eyes and shaking her whole body with glee. So, sorry Kalpana this issue isn’t about you but it is about the political concerns, struggles, hopes, rage and desperations we shared as friends, saathis and Sahelis... so in that sense, we think you’ll approve. On a more serious note though, this is a very difficult piece to write. As Savita said, ‘It’s impossible to put 40 years of friendship into words.’ But the real challenge is even bigger than that: Kalpana wasn’t just a friend, a saathi, a founder member of Saheli, she was a force of nature – loud, warm, wonderful, vibrant, fearless, loving, emotional, unpredictable, systematic, funny, determined, experienced, anadi (naïve)... and much more. As a young woman, Kalpana was doing her MBA in the U.S. after completing her B. Tech in Aeronautical Engineering from IIT-Kanpur when the Emergency was declared. When she returned to India in 1976, the country was still reeling under its impact. After a few years with trade unions, Kalpana joined other women from the Left and socialist movements as they started to organize themselves on issues confronting women – in what has since come to be known as the autonomous women’s movement of the late 1970s and early 1980s. An important part of this history is the founding of Saheli Women’s Resource Centre in Delhi on 9 August 1981, by ‘8 women – Amiya Rao, Bharati Roy Chaudhry, Buchy aka Lakshmi, Gouri Chowdhry, Kalpana Mehta, Rukmini Rao, Vichitra, Vidya Rao – with 80 rupees, two jhadoos, one notebook, a flyswatter and the strength of their convictions’, as the legend goes. Ashima recalls, ‘It was early 1981 when I faced the first big challenge of my life. My marriage had crumbled, I had no job, and all that I could call my own including my clothes, personal effects and money in a joint bank account were out of reach. I also didn’t have anyone to turn to for advice and comfort except my parents. That is when my father took me to meet his youngest brother and sister-in-law, Gouri Chowdhury. That was on 4 August 1981, just a few days before Saheli was formally inaugurated. It was the day I met a bunch of young women who listened keenly to this very unhappy, confused and stressed out female. Their empathy and patience had a huge effect on me: this was the comfort zone which I had been searching for. Among the few who stood out for me was Kalpana. Somehow I was convinced that I had found my pillars of strength. During the period that followed – of a new job, receiving divorce summons in the office, finances in doldrums, making daily trips to Saheli office in Nizamuddin after work, the going got tougher. There were many moments when I would burst into tears. One day Kalpana took me outside the Saheli office and hugged me till I stopped crying. Since then she was always there when I needed advice and guidance, and her home was where I went to relax and spend some happy times. Of course, I got a lot of strength from other Saheli members too – together they helped me rebuild my tattered life. Savita remembers that in 1981 when she came to Saheli seeking help on her personal crisis, the office would
            open only in the evenings. Like Ashima, Savita too became part of Saheli, and was in fact, the group’s first full
            timer dealing with other women’s problems: going to the police station with them, dealing with dowry death
            cases, following up on FIRs and medical reports. ‘Kalpana had the ability to spot talent and channelize it. She
            encouraged me to do all this, and even to write about these experiences for the first Saheli newsletter,’ reminisces
            Savita, who still has to be cajoled into writing so many years later (clearly, we don’t all have Kalpana’s charm!). It was soon after the 1984 riots that Ramani came to Saheli. ‘I met Kalpana, Elizabeth Vatsyayan and Nalini Bhanot
            – they were the regulars at Saheli. Ashima Roy Chowdhry, Ranjana Padhi, Savita Sharma, Rukmini Rao, Sadhna
            Arya, Sujata Madhok, Laxmi Murthy, Nilanjana Mukherjee and Malati Rao would also come on some days. It was
            a very interactive and cohesive group. Saheli did case-work those days, so they taught me how to talk to women
            in distress and write daily case-diaries. We also had weekly study classes about feminist issues and politics. I left
            Saheli after a few years when I started teaching full time. When I returned after nearly a decade, the affection
            and welcome I got from Kalpana and everyone else made me feel so much at home. This openness of all Sahelis
            is what makes the group so special.’ ‘I always saw Kalpana as very confident, courageous, intelligent, and sharp in her Left and feminist politics,”says
            Sadhna. “Once she was convinced of something, she would lose no time in going ahead with it even if it invited
            criticism or made some people unhappy. In the first Saheli publication titled, The First Four Years, Kalpana writes,
            ’I come because I belong. It is not always love and warmth, it is fights and bickering as well. It is not always the
            work I think I should be doing – but then I belong HERE, with all other Sahelis, so I come... One breathes Saheli
            and sometimes it is breath of fresh air and at others... small rewards keep you growing and keep your faith in
            “try and try again”. There are times of stress and distrust, times of peak activity and discovering togetherness...
            Something we share is the courage to swim together against the tide – whether it is on the Egalitarian Civil Code
            or opposing population control, the penny pinching in our work and the chaos in which we function.’ Decades
            later Kalpana’s words ring true for most of us – through all the emotional bursts, highs and lows of being a Saheli. ‘She was genuinely caring towards anyone who was troubled, but on the flip side, she could be very tough and
            could hurt people,’ remembers Ashima. ‘I will never forget that during a weekly meeting, everyone was being
            asked to commit more time to Saheli work, and I said I couldn’t. Kalpana said I should work in Saheli during my
            next annual leave and not go off traversing to some foreign land. After much arguments and mediation I agreed,
            but I was angry. But over time, I understood that it was her dedication to Saheli and the women’s movement that
            drove her to push me that way.’ Sadhna notes, ’Kalpana understood that as a small organisation, we need to strategise to take our perspective/s
            forward, connect with struggles of working class women, and engage with mass based organisations like AIDWA,
            NFIW, etc., be part of struggles against displacement and its impact on women be they because of “conflict” or
            “development”. In fact, at the event marking 25 years of Saheli, she spoke passionately about the need for metro
            based women’s groups to connect more deeply with groups and women in smaller towns. Equally, she believed
            that institutions of the state should be held accountable. ‘Until we organise women on a wider basis, the most
            we can do is to act as a vigilant body, to see that these institutions/forces are used to protect rather than exploit
            the oppressed. The need is to extend ourselves – increase our collective strength.’ So it was no surprise that she
            was an integral part of planning and implementing a sit-in inside the office of the Drugs Controller of India (DCI)
            against hazardous long acting contraceptives, leading a protest into the NCW office to demand the report on jail
            conditions of Soni Sori and others, compelling the NCW team to visit a displacement site in Madhya Pradesh, or
            the Cover-Up Campaign, in which we dumped countless bedsheets with political messages at the CBI headquarters
            for their “next cover-up” after they wilfully botched up the Shopian double rape and murder investigation. ‘‘Her zest for life took the form of delightful subversions as political strategy,’
            remembers Vani. ‘When I first started coming to Saheli, the group was in the
            throws of the campaign against EP drugs (High dose combination hormonal
            pills and injections that were wrongly and harmfully used to diagnose
            pregnancy). The government’s claim was that since it was supposedly
            available only on prescription, its (mis)use was controlled. To call out their
            lie, one strategy was for us to collect fake prescriptions and buy the drug
            over the counter with the name of the DCI as the prescribing doctor! To
            me, a neophyte in feminist politics, this seemed like too daring a move. But
            the Sahelis would just crack up with delight every time one of us came in
            with more ‘evidence’ that strengthened our case. And then of course was

            the historic ‘let’s-leap-over-the-walls-and-bust-a-public-relations-press-
            conference-on-Depo-Provera moment’. These may of course, have been

            the very moments when I fell in love with this group of badmaash aurtein
            called Saheli.’   ‘After being in Delhi for 3-4 years one day in 1994, I went to Saheli to pick up
            a parcel that had been left for me,’ remembers Vineeta. ‘A group of women
            happily chatted with me and extended an open invitation to come to Saheli
            whenever I felt like. I have no recollection of who I met during that first
            visit, but I soon started dropping in, and before I realised it, I was roped
            into discussions, participating in meetings, and became a Saheli. Eventually
            I came to know Kalpana, Elizabeth, Laxmi, Ranjana, Sadhna, Vani better.
            But it was Kalpana who took me under her wing, as was her wont. She was
            warm, hospitable and often invited me to stay back at her place after Saheli
            meetings. Late night discussions, arguments about nuclear weapons and
            nuclear energy, contraceptive devices, vaccines, including anti-hCG vaccine
            as a contraceptive followed – while we agreed on the goal we were working
            towards, we often had strong disagreements about how we should get there.
            I was quite naive on the issue of population control, but Kalpana helped me
            get a grasp of it. Despite my inadequacies she asked me to help revise Saheli’s
            primer on women’s health and contraceptives [fondly described as the ‘Red
            Book’!]. Saheli’s work in women’s reproductive health helped me develop a
            feminist perspective on contraception and women’s health, and opened my
            eyes to the lack of social and economic understanding of health issues as
            they are taught in medical college.’ Besides Saheli, Kalpana was involved in the conceptualisation and setting
            up of several other feminist initiatives. ‘Paridhi’asought to research and
            manufacture diaphragms as part of a larger feminist search for effective
            barrier methods of contraception that would be healthy, safe and in the
            control of women themselves. She set up ‘Manasi’with a group of health
            activists and doctors to provide health care from traditional healing systems
            as well as allopathy. She was also a trained Reiki master who used the practice
            to heal others, as well as on herself, once she contracted the immensely
            debilitating ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, one type ofmotor neuron
            disease) which eventually took her away. ‘One thing that perplexed me about Kalpana was her increasing dependence
            on and use of alternative forms of medicine such as Reiki. How could
            somebody, who waded through piles and piles of references and collected
            scientific information to counter the arguments made by those who forced
            hazardous contraceptives on women, start believing in forms of medicine where evidence for their use is still lacking?’ says Vineeta. ‘In the early 2000s when
            I joined Saheli, Kalpana was a name you read in the ‘First 4 Years’ booklet. As I
            stayed longer, it seemed that Kalpana was more a historical figure and less a real
            one, quoted here in a souvenir, there in a newsletter. As my involvement with Saheli
            deepened, I was sure that Kalpana was actually a concept, a feminist principle.
            When you meet such a figure in person you do what many younger feminists have
            done and will continue to do – challenge them, their methods... it’s inevitable. 20
            years later, I wish this had not been the case,’ muses Deepti. But differences weren’t
            what made or broke relationships with Kalpana. She had the ability to rise above
            them and reach out if she sensed unhappiness in someone; she could get up from
            an acrimonious Saheli meeting, and invite you over to share a drink, have a laugh,
            and continue the argument, of course! As Savita says, the ‘relationship with her was
            always both, political and familial.’ In the first decade of the 2000s, a small but determined group including Kalpana was
            instrumental in setting up Women Against Sexual Violence and State Repression
            (WSS) – a national level feminist response to the increasing use of sexual violence
            as a means of state repression – an attempt to address the failure of the mainstream
            women’s movement to respond adequately to the issue. The national canvas of the
            network, the range of activists and movements it drew together, brought Kalpana’s
            organisational and inter-personal skills to the fore once again, and gave her renewed
            strength and energy. ‘Kalpana was always methodical and determined, but I am especially inspired by how
            she stayed politically engaged till the very end’ remembers Satnam. An apt tribute
            to a woman who beat the odds of her health condition to stay totally updated on
            issues till her last moments: raging against the CAA-NRC-NPR project; challenging
            the detention camps and saying, ‘I want to be a doubtful citizen and have them look
            after me in my current situation’; and signing a petition for the release of anti-CAA
            activists wrongly charged for sedition, just a day before she passed on. In closing, a lovely memory: After the Saheli office was burnt down by a fire in 2009,
            we decided to gather in the office to get our energies back. In the crowd room, we
            all, Sahelis and friends of Saheli, sat together laughing, crying, talking over each
            other. And there she was, Kalpana sitting in the middle of everyone, singing – Mein
            Zindagi ka saath nibhata chala gaya, har fikr ko dhooyen mein udaata chala gaya... Zindabad Kalpana. It’s hard to think of you in the past tense, but your work and its
            legacy lives on. They really don’t make them like you any more.

Vidya Bal, or Vidya tai to many, especially in Maharashtra, was a feminist icon, popular magazine editor and founder of several political initiatives in her long and eventful life. But for us in Saheli, she was simply and amazingly, just Vidya. Loved by all of us not just because her daughter Vineeta has been a long time Saheli, but because Vidya’s warm and loving persona was a perfect complement to her sharp political convictions. As a tiny group that struggles to publish a bi-annual newsletter, we were totally floored when she shared how she and her group publish the monthly magazine, Miloon Saryajani, consistently since 9 August 1989 (coincidentally on Saheli’s eight anniversary!).  We felt the strength of her spirit when she spoke out fearlessly against the targeted killing of the eminent rationalist, Narendra Dabholkar, only to find herself facing death threats at almost the age of 80! Vidya was inspiring in many ways too. She reconfigured the famed feminist slogan of ‘personal is political’ by proving that ‘political can go far beyond the personal’. Many instances come to mind. When Vidya realised she didn’t know enough about emerging LGBTQI+ issues, she chose to engage with those who could help her understand and teach her, before she stepped out in support and even led the Pune Pride. Vidya also led a legal battle for women’s right to enter the sanctum sanctorum of the Shani Shingnapur temple, even though she was herself an avowed atheist. That’s the kind of feminism not everyone can believe in, much less, live. But Vidya did, and we’ll always be inspired by that. You are missed far beyond the state of Maharashtra, Vidya. With much love, from all of us in Saheli, New Delhi.

Ilina Sen portrait Ilina’s life and work were dedicated to making meaningful linkages between women’s movements challenging patriarchal oppression, and peoples’ movements struggling for livelihood, as well as the sustainability of natural resources of jal, jangal and zameen. For many years, Ilina chose to be with marginalised and oppressed communities and workers in the political battle for their rights, but also to live with and learn from them. She taught adivasi children, was an integral part of public health movements, trade unions, human rights and adivasi/tribal organisations. Her pathbreaking work, A Space Within the Struggle – Women’s Participation in People’s Struggles chronicles the struggles of brick workers, landless labourers, fishworkers, etc., people who still often remain invisible to the discipline of women’s studies; and continues to be a pioneering work on understanding women’s participation in people’s struggles and their fight to bring women’s perspectives to these struggles. Ilina's later work Sukhwasin: The Migrant Woman of Chhattisgarh on the issue of migration out of Chhattisgarh due to drought, famine and hunger, threw special light on the conditions of migrant women. Thus, long before she joined the Gender Studies Departments in Mahatma Gandhi Antarrashtriya Hindi University, Wardha, and later the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, and becoming President, Indian Association of Women Studies, she was writing and thinking about the intersectionality of struggles. Ilina’s soft demeanor concealed her firm resolve to fight for justice. Her personal and political struggles became inextricably intermeshed when her husband and fellow activist Binayak Sen was arrested and charged with the UAPA. She fought relentlessly, not just for his release but also against the abysmal conditions and overcrowding in Indian prisons. Despite failing health, she never faltered in her determination to resist anti-people public health and development policies, attempts to quash dissent, rampant human rights violations, laws against sedition, and so on. The sweetness with which Ilina would render songs of women’s and peoples’ rights movements still lingers with us. Her determination and clarity of purpose still inspires us. Zindabad, Ilina.
contentHi: इलिना सेन का चित्र इलिना का जीवन और कार्य पितृसत्तात्मक उत्पीड़न को चुनौती देने वाले महिला आंदोलनों और आजीविका के लिए संघर्षरत जन आंदोलनों के बीच सार्थक संबंध बनाने के लिए समर्पित था, साथ ही जल, जंगल और जमीन जैसे प्राकृतिक संसाधनों की स्थिरता के लिए भी। कई वर्षों तक इलिना ने हाशिए पर रह रहे और उत्पीड़ित समुदायों और मजदूरों के साथ उनके अधिकारों की राजनीतिक लड़ाई में भाग लिया, उनके साथ रहकर और उनसे सीखते हुए। उन्होंने आदिवासी बच्चों को पढ़ाया, सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य आंदोलनों, ट्रेड यूनियनों, मानवाधिकार और आदिवासी संगठनों में सक्रिय भूमिका निभाई। उनका महत्वपूर्ण कार्य *A Space Within the Struggle – Women’s Participation in People’s Struggles* ईंट भट्ठा मजदूरों, भूमिहीन मजदूरों, मछुआरों आदि के संघर्षों का दस्तावेज है — वे लोग जो अक्सर महिला अध्ययन के क्षेत्र में अदृश्य रह जाते हैं। यह पुस्तक जन आंदोलनों में महिलाओं की भागीदारी और उन आंदोलनों में महिलाओं के दृष्टिकोण को सामने लाने के संघर्ष को समझने में अग्रणी मानी जाती है। इलिना का बाद का कार्य *Sukhwasin: The Migrant Woman of Chhattisgarh* सूखा, अकाल और भूख के कारण छत्तीसगढ़ से होने वाले पलायन और प्रवासी महिलाओं की स्थितियों पर विशेष प्रकाश डालता है। महात्मा गांधी अंतरराष्ट्रीय हिंदी विश्वविद्यालय, वर्धा के जेंडर स्टडीज़ विभाग और बाद में टाटा सामाजिक विज्ञान संस्थान से जुड़ने तथा भारतीय महिला अध्ययन संघ की अध्यक्ष बनने से बहुत पहले ही वे संघर्षों की अंतर्संबद्धता पर लिख और सोच रही थीं। इलिना के सौम्य स्वभाव के पीछे न्याय के लिए संघर्ष करने का उनका अडिग संकल्प छिपा था। उनके व्यक्तिगत और राजनीतिक संघर्ष तब गहराई से एक-दूसरे से जुड़ गए जब उनके पति और साथी कार्यकर्ता बिनायक सेन को यूएपीए के तहत गिरफ्तार किया गया। उन्होंने न केवल उनकी रिहाई के लिए बल्कि भारतीय जेलों की दयनीय और भीड़भाड़ वाली परिस्थितियों के खिलाफ भी निरंतर संघर्ष किया। बिगड़ती सेहत के बावजूद वे जनविरोधी सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य और विकास नीतियों, असहमति को दबाने के प्रयासों, मानवाधिकार उल्लंघनों और देशद्रोह जैसे कानूनों के खिलाफ डटी रहीं। महिलाओं और जन अधिकार आंदोलनों के गीतों को जिस मधुरता से इलिना गाया करती थीं, उसकी गूंज आज भी हमारे साथ है। उनका दृढ़ संकल्प और उद्देश्य की स्पष्टता आज भी हमें प्रेरित करती है। ज़िंदाबाद, इलिना।

contentEn: It's late 2016. We are on the opening panel of the North India Regional Conference of the IAWS on, 'Documenting Women's Experiences in the Movement: Issues, Experiences and Struggles' in Ranchi. A number of questions confront us. How to present an overview of more than thirty-five years of an activist group? Which accounts can best illustrate the twists and turns of our many campaigns, many journeys? What reflections can generate useful discussions on what's been gained and lost over the decades? What contemplations on our organisational structure and functioning should we focus on? What narratives can make meaningful contribution to contemporary debates and questions of women's movements in India that we have gathered here to discuss today? Asked to focus on our work related to women's health, we frame those campaigns within the rubric of violence against women by corporations and the State. Reflecting on how those strategies find resonance in other campaigns targeted against the State as well as communal, sectarian, misogynist, homophobic forces in society, we bring within the ambit of the discussion, our commitment to generating vibrant debates with friends and comrades in our shared struggles. Because like most feminists we believe that change starts from within. But first, a brief backgrounder - Saheli started in New Delhi in 1981 primarily as a crisis intervention centre. Like many of the earliest autonomous groups in the country, our struggles against oppression and violence within marriage, family and community led to vibrant campaigns against dowry, domestic violence, rape, sexual harassment, communalism, war, and discrimination against women in the law. Our work on women's health involved long standing campaigns against coercive population control policies, hazardous contraceptives, sex-determination, the unethical sale of emergency    contraceptives, and vaccines against cervical cancer. Not surprisingly, the challenges have been many and complex, and so have been our strategies to confront them. Since the late 1970s, when women's groups began to publicly challenge violence against women it was the first step to breaking the silence surrounding it, visibilising it and taking it out of the 'private' domain to make it a public concern. Thus, while challenging the violence of one citizen against another, we exposed the structures that sustain (and even legitimise) such violence: the power of patriarchy, the inequities of gender, the oppression of women within institutions of marriage, family and community, and of course, most critically, the State and its institutions. Be it in the cases of dowry related murders such as that of Sudha Goel, or Kanchanbala, the daughter of that fiery activist, Satyarani Chaddha; the 'Sati' murder of Roop Kanwar of Deorala or even, decades later, that of Charanshah of Mahoba. But well before these legendary battles of the autonomous women's movements came to be, by the turn of 1980, a series of instances of custodial violence - the rape of a young Adivasi woman in Maharashtra, Mathura (and the subsequent acquittal of the guilty by the Supreme Court); the sexual assault and parading of Maya Tyagi in Baghpat District, and Rameeza Bee in Hyderabad, among others - catalysed the coming together of many feminist groups across the country as autonomous women's 'movements', as we prefer to call ourselves today. So, what does it mean for Saheli to be autonomous? When Saheli came into being, it was a time when women from many Left parties, socialist formations and people's movements were seeking political spaces that would be more responsive to women and women's issues. We were talking about what affected us as women — in such a context, our organisational autonomy from both, political parties and the State, was and remains, central. Likewise on funding, we maintain our distance from institutional agendas and support, both Indian and international. While members have 'other' jobs/ occupations to earn their living, we sustain our organisational work through individual donations, periodic fund raising efforts and contributions gathered against publications. This autonomy is reflected in our choice of work and strategy, as much as it informs our effort to work outside the framework of hierarchical structures, as a feminist collective, with all its strengths and limitations. One of the important legacies of feminist activism is the refusal to be intimidated by the power of any 'specialised' knowledge, be it legal, medical or economic. As our work as a crisis intervention centre helped us uncover the gender biases in laws and cultural practices across communities, we engaged with religious personal laws, customary practices, secular laws, and the gender biases of the legal and judicial machinery. Every intervention in the arena of law/legal reform - be it sexual assault, representation of women in the media, domestic violence, Section 377 of the IPC, communal violence, changes in Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), the Sexual Assault Bill or in fact even the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act that emerged after a nationwide campaign against sex selective abortions - has required us to develop specific areas of knowledge and expertise within the group as the foundation on which we build a collective understanding and take a position on the matter.  Over time, our understanding of violence on women became more expansive, recognising women's health as a political site of violence by the State. Consider this - the period of the Emergency from 1975-1977 is recognised for widespread violence and repression by the State which included, among its horrors, the forced sterilisations of men in camps. Ever since the period of the Emergency, the focus of the State's family planning policies and programmes has shifted entirely to the women of this country whose health and wellbeing has been systematically jeopardised by the State, its institutions and policies through coercive population control, forced, unsafe and early sterilisations, and unethical trials on poor, Dalit and Adivasi women and girls of hazardous long-acting, hormonal contraceptives like Net-En, Norplant and Depo Provera, chemical sterilisation methods such as Quinacrine, vaccines against cervical cancer. Countless actions of the State that fall firmly within the rubric of violence on women, that have led to robust campaigns against them by Saheli, along with other autonomous groups as well as Left party affiliated organisations such as All Indian Democratic Women's Association (AIDWA) and the National Federation of Indian Women (NFIW). Since the early 1980s, we mounted a firm resistance to the introduction of hazardous contraceptives, the lack of information, and sheer misinformation, campaigns surrounding them as well as unethical trials by State institutions such as the Indian Council for Medical Research (ICMR) that ironically, sets the ethical standards for trials on human subjects, while itself flagrantly violating them! And our strategies to do so were multifarious: in addition to leaflets, posters, plays and dharnas, when Hyderabad-based Stree Shakti Sanghatna discovered that women at a health camp were being deceived into participating in trials of Net-En, we were part of the protests that spread all over the country and culminated with us taking the ICMR and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to court in 1986. When Norplant was sought to be introduced through trials on about eighty thousand women we built a huge public resistance by demystifying its 'science' in the public domain, even creating a street play on the politics of population control, raising the issue with other women's groups and democratic rights groups to build a stronger support base for the campaign. At the international level too, we demanded that our feminist sisters make a paradigm shift to place what was happening to women's health in developing nations within global politics of population control, corporate and State interests in controlling women's fertility.  For instance, in the early years of globalisation, Saheli along with many other Delhi-based women's groups, mounted a historic resistance to the introduction of Depo-Provera in India by taking over a press conference organised by the Max Pharma and its public relations agency, Mudra Diversified. The coordinated protest (along with its precursor in Mumbai) broke headlines all over the country and had a deterrent impact on the promotion/prescription of Depo Provera for many years. But today, with Depo Provera being approved for introduction into the Family Planning Programme, this anecdote gets relegated to the annals of nostalgia and history of the women's health movement. But in fact, it stands as a reminder of how complex battles against hazardous contraceptives have become in the post liberalisation 'free market', especially with widespread corporatisation of the media, where fewer and fewer stories of State or corporation (ir)responsibility find any place. The truth is that when even the most hazardous contraceptives and vaccines are marketed as 'free choice', we are hard-pressed to find a language that helps women see past these euphemisms, and find ways to safeguard their health, understand their sexuality, control their fertility and other life choices. Since 1981, when Saheli was formally registered, we have waxed and waned in numbers but our organisational structure has remained that of a collective. We make decisions by consensus, have no formal hierarchy, and our only concession to leadership is the unenviable rotational job of being a monthly coordinator. Also related to this is the idea of the collective as the choice to challenge patriarchal and institutional hierarchies, the idea that notions like equality and care need to be reflected not just in our political goals but in the means to those goals, thus requiring us to consistently interrogate the structures of power and inequality that exist between us as a part of our larger feminist struggle. As a small collective, Saheli understands that its greater strength lies in its collective action with others. So we join hands with like-minded groups and individuals on a range of campaigns: struggling with student groups to Reclaim the Night or for a Safe Campus in Delhi University; being part of platforms like the Dilli Janwaadi Adhikaar Manch on factory closures and workers' rights; working with democratic rights groups and anti-nuclear platforms against war, nuclear energy and militarisation in the north east. (One of the most long-standing feminist voices against militarised responses of the State to political conflict, Saheli has been central to struggles against draconian laws like the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA), the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), or even the gross misuse of the Indian Penal Code in states like Chhattisgarh.) We have a long history of working on wider platforms for peace and democracy. In solidarity with the struggles of activists like Irom Sharmila. In the face of communal conflicts - Delhi 1984 and 1992/3, Gujarat 2002, and Muzaffarnagar 2013. In the last few years, as part of the Women against Sexual Violence and State Repression (WSS) network we have worked on the widespread sexual violence on Dalit women and girls in Haryana. In the case of custodial torture of Adivasi activist Soni Sori or the hounding out of human rights lawyers from Chhattisgarh, together we have employed a mix of strategies - the power of street action, going to the courts, conducting fact findings, flooding the social media with information, mobilising national and international press - especially because the State in Chhattisgarh has no place for dissent, and the local press is either biased, scared or simply inflammatory against activists and human rights defenders. (As we write this, the Chhattisgarh Special Public Security Act has been invoked on seven human rights activists from Telangana on a fact-finding visit to Sukhma!). But every once in a while, when faced with the absolute refusal of the State to act in the course of justice, we are compelled to push ourselves to think of more creative ways to generate public awareness of the atrocities of the State. When the rape and murder of two young women allegedly by the Indian army in Shopian shook Jammu and Kashmir in 2009, and fact-finding missions, repeatedly implicated State agencies in the cover up to protect defence personnel, WSS launched the CBI: Cover-Up Bureau of India Campaign. A tongue in cheek mobilisation that resulted in us 'gifting' the CBI hundreds of bed-sheets with slogans against its dubious role in the Shopian investigation!  As activists, the dissemination of our ideas, politics and perspectives has always been a challenge. So at Saheli, women's 'study' and 'activism' have never been binary opposites. From the start, our activism has been sustained by research, feminist analysis, writing and dissemination. And so it is, Saheli is one of the very few autonomous women's groups with a long history of publishing: a (reasonably regular) newsletter in English and Hindi; fact finding reports, research reports, plays, leaflets, posters, booklets, the works. In the area of women's health for instance, we published a series of monographs on contraceptive and sterilisation methods, challenging their claims to safety and efficacy, and even guidebook on reproductive knowledge for young women (our very own Red Book), long before the language of 'sexuality' and 'choice' came to us. Then, there have been research studies and a play on sexual harassment at the workplace, and periodic publications that recap, review and reflect on Saheli's work over the years. In recent years, we have also been archiving older debates, creating online access to reports, newsletters, leaflets, posters and other published materials created over the decades. (Check out www.saheliwomen.org, or reach out to us at saheliwomen@gmail.com) Take for instance, the study we undertook in the aftermath of the communal carnage of Muslims in Gujarat. Shaken by the widespread participation of women in the violence, we felt the need to understand how women are socialised into ideas of belonging to family and community (religious or otherwise), and how, their role as carriers of culture can feed into the kind of religious polarisation that we witnessed in 2002. This, despite the fact that it is women who bear the brunt of most cultural norms and mores! Around the same period, Saheli had also been engaging with issues and interlinkages between caste and gender, the power of patriarchy in maintaining caste hierarchies. (As a matter of fact, we later coordinated the Session on Women & Caste at the National Conference of Autonomous Women's Movements in Kolkata in 2006 with CADAM and Sama.) So we embarked on a study of how patriarchal institutions like marriage and family control women's sexuality, and explored its intersections with caste, community, class and religious identities. We spoke to women both within and outside the institution of marriage, women who had entered it through 'love' or family based arrangements, had crossed caste and community borders in doing so, or those who had stayed/become single, as well as some who were completely outside its ambit, like lesbian women. The results of this complex study were then published in 2007 as a report titled, Talking Marriage, Caste and Community: Voices from Within.  While the report holds its own even today, we soon faced the question of how to take such complex discussions out into the public domain, in ways beyond the classical 'presentation' or 'talk'. We wanted to generate discussions and debates that would encourage reflections on women's relationships with families, communities, and cultures. And at the same time, create awareness of how these factors determine our constructions of 'otherness'. This dilemma then led to us to where Sahelis often end up: the creation of a new play called Kaun Jaat that sought to question categories of 'aurat jaat/mard jaat', 'unchi jaat/ neechi jaat', 'apni jaat/doosri jaat', and so on. A play in 5 monologues, Kaun Jaat featured a young woman Sapna in an arranged marriage, Rashmi/Reshma in an interreligious love marriage; Meenakshi, a Dalit doctor in a premium medical institute; Leena, a lesbian woman in an inter-caste relationship; and Bilkis/Manorama/Surekha/Sister M: a victim of communal/State violence who was sexually assaulted and/or killed because of their identity. All, not surprisingly, from marginalised communities - Dalit, Muslim, Christian and Tribal from the North East. All, attacked because of their gender, caste and community. All, made vulnerable by the deep-rooted patriarchal Brahmanism that creates and dominates the idea of the nation. As the satirical chorus of a song in the play set to a popular Hindi film track goes: Over time, the play (and its excerpted monologues) has become a powerful tool to generate discussions on these complex intersectionalities in colleges, at seminars, and even among comrade groups working to widen the ambit of 'the right to choice' beyond inter-caste and inter-religious alliances to same sex relationships. After all, we learn from each others' struggles and each others' trajectories of growth. Thirty-five years on, Saheli is still in 'act'ivist mode, despite a slowing down of autonomous energies and politics across the nation. A challenge that has multiplied many fold with the State and street crackdown on all voices of dissent, attacks on secularists, people's movements, NGOs, students and marginalised communities, most often under the guise of the 'national good' and 'national security'. These are paradigms we need to challenge together today. We must strengthen our work with other movements to build resistance against the violations and excesses of the State, corporations and other vested powers in society, especially casteist and fundamentalist assertions of the right wing in every aspect of life. Only then can we hope to come closer to the idea of creating an egalitarian society where everyone can live with courage, justice and hope. Together.

contentEn: Are you a feminist, or do you wonder whether you are? Does the phrase 'question authority' make you raise your fist in the air? Do you sing badly? Does the idea of being a part of an autonomous women's group (and finally the movement) excite you? Do you think independently, but can work collectively? Do you see political work as extending to the upkeep of a certain hot-dusty-quivering-under-the-traffic-flyover office? Do you believe that our struggles are intrinsically intertwined, and the liberation of women lies in the liberation of all from brahminical, patriarchal forces? 1+1 = 11, right? Is alliance-building/solidarity with others who are struggling, a central part of your politics? Are you willing to question yourself and us about dearly-held beliefs? Do you want to work on campaigns and not projects? Do you have nothing better to do on a Saturday? Do you think some of the above are inside jokes that you want in on? We could go on... but if you like where the above questions take you, then it's time for you to drop us an email and come by under the flyover on any Saturday so we can get to know each other over chai, licking stamps, bill payments, heated discussions, menstrual cramps and other such joys.

contentEn: After the fire Saheli got a lot of support - love that we can not keep accounts of, help with running around and a lot of financial support too! In all we received Rs 6,95,440 for rebuilding our office, to have it furnished and for replenishing our materials. For a long time we were waiting for a go ahead by the pWD who was to repair and declare the superstructure safe. We waited for more than one year but the PWD did not even start any repairs and of course we had no permission to go ahead. In the meanwhile the remaining establishments under the flyover rebuilt their offices and shops. After waiting for one year we also renovated our office. Instead of the two rooms earlier we now have one large space with a moveable partition, that can be used for big meetings and when necessary we can use the space as two rooms. You may recall that immediately after the fire we had made a temporary structure and put up windows to prevent vandalism and takeover and we had sent you pictures of the same. some of the money was used at that time. The full account of what has been spent is as follows: To secure the office with windows door and wall - RS 66,357. 2012-13 For reconstruction and furnishing - RS 4,09,432. We are yet to buy a computer and some furniture but since last saheli day we have been using the office space. since most of the major expenses have been taken care of we are sharing this information and once again thanking you all. Here is a glimpse of our office now.
