titleEn: THEATRE AS TEXTS OF THE WOMEN’S MOVEMENT
subtitle: A Presentation
contentEn: [The following is a version of a presentation that was made by Saheli at Ambedkar University, as part of the MA Gender Studies course module. The presentation started with the unmistakable 'He ji re', included video clips from performances of 'Kaun Jaat' and 'Mahaul Badalna Hai' and led to nearly three hours of wonderful discussions with students, questions and answers, and more songs!] How does theatre form a text for the women's movement? Answering this question would require us to look at street plays in specific, and the ways in which street plays lend themselves to use in social movements, and the women's movement in particular. We talked briefly about some of the plays that we had used and had experiences of in Saheli, and then discussed the kind of issues they talk about, as well as the process of creating the plays and performing them actually tells us about the movements and the campaigns that they were a part of. These were 'Om Swaha', a play on dowry deaths that was part of the anti-dowry campaign of the 1980s, 'Norplant', a play on the dangers of contraceptives, part of  the health campaign, 'Mahaul Badalna Hai', a play about sexual harassment at the workplace designed to spread awareness about the Vishakha Guidelines, and 'Kaun Jaat', a play that was born out of the need to understand interconnections in the various axes of exploitation. Street plays have long been a part of the folk culture in the Indian subcontinent, and been used by social movements in India as well to great effect. Typically loud, energetic and engaging performances given by actors, these plays seek to convey messages of critique and change in a simple way, through humour and songs. However, when it comes to the women's movement, street plays assume a greater significance. Firstly, street plays quite straightforwardly enable the aspect of accessing public space and bringing what is often considered to be private out into the public sphere, something feminist movements have always tried to do through various campaigns and issues. Most significantly, this can be seen in issues of violence against women, which has always been categorised as 'ghar ka maamla' or a private family issue, especially when ideas of shame and honour are invoked. The challenge has been to speak about it in public, in part to remove the stigma from the vich'm and also to enable the perpetrator to be punished, both in a social and legal sense. 'Om Swaha' was a play that belonged to the strong anti-dowry campaign of the 1980s, which took up the issue of dowry deaths and forced it into the public consciousness at a time when nobody was talking about dowry violence, when it was brushed away as a private matter. The campaign was widespread all over most of North India, as well as Maharashtra, with protests and demonstrations, all driven by the need to break the silence around dowry.  The play begins with the auctioning of young men, a comic scene to show the humiliation and harassment that women undergo when they are placed on the "marriage market". It then picks up the story of a young woman, starting from her birth to her marriage, and addressing the ill treatment she receives at the hands of her in-laws for failing to bring adequate dowry. Her parents refuse to take her back. For the last scene, the performers would break the fourth wall and ask the audience to choose between two versions of the last scene - the first, where the woman dies of violence in her husband's house or the second, where she stands up for her rights and ultimately leaves the house and is able to successfully get on with her life. Both versions would then be performed in order to bring out the pathos of the first scenario. The play was interspersed with Punjabi folk songs, in order to form a connection with the audience, as the locus of the anti-dowry movement was largely around Delhi, the site of highest instances of dowry related violence. However, the play was also translated and performed in many other parts of the country as well. 'Om Swaha' was performed over 300 times in the 1980's. It added to the urgency of the anti-dowry movement, as play performances became a way for women to speak out about the violence in their homes, and approach women groups for help. The play performed the dual purpose of not only bringing the issue into public dialogue, but also making the audience, and all of society by extension, responsible for ending the social evil of dowry. Another significance of street plays we discussed was the effects of simply capturing a public place. Typically street plays are performed in marketplaces, on streets outside bastis or factories, on a busy lawn in a college, in a bustling street. Such places which are typically hostile to women, when playing host to a troupe of noisy, colourful women collecting an audience and performing for them, undergo a transformation - they become a space of dialogue, where women's issues are brought up into examination, where the possibility of change becomes real and shared. At the very least for the duration of the play's performance, the nature of public space itself becomes charged with a different kind of energy.  Coming to the issues of women in the public space, the Supreme Court guidelines on the issue of sexual harassment at the workplace in 1997, which came to be known as the 'Vishakha guidelines', were the first of its kind in the country to define the ambit of sexual harassment faced by women, and marked the first time that the government acknowledged that workplaces could be hostile and discriminatory to women. About a year after the guidelines came out, Saheli conducted a survey of women working in various fields of employment regarding their experiences in a hostile working environment and the kinds of harassment they faced. Following the survey, Saheli released a report in 1998, titled "Another Occupafional Hazard: Sexual Harassment at the Workplace". The findings of the survey pointed to three important things: first, the lack of recognition and trivialisation of the problem of sexual harassment at the workplace; second, the blaming of the victim for her own harassment; and third, the fact that while almost all women in all sectors experienced sexual harassment, the extent and nature of the violence was directly linked to their class, nature of the work, location of the work, level of job security, and so on. These were serious issues that needed to be addressed along with the need to spread awareness about the guidelines. Saheli had also worked on some cases of sexual harassment, which reinforced our feeling that we needed a concerted campaign. And so the idea of doing a street play was born. The play 'Mahaul Badalna Hai' features 5 characters, all working women, who face differing degrees of harassment in their workplaces. An important device we evolved in the play is to not show the perpetrators of the harassment, as all too often, scenes of harassment become used for a voyeuristic and titillating effect, or if acted not too well, even hilarity! So, in effect, each scene simply has one side of a conversation - showing the woman going about her daily work, experiencing escalating provocation or attacks, and her reactions to it all, yet the presence of the harassers is all too ominous. The larger issue of women's ownership of their bodies and their right not to be harassed is conveyed through two contrasting scenes. The first is a scene of victim blaming, where the woman who is complaining of being harassed is told it is her fault for wearing certain kinds of clothes, or overreacting to simple teasing, or even merely stepping out of the house to find work. The second, an ironic parallel, has a man whose wallet is stolen on the street and faces similar taunts from the onlookers; that it is the man's fault for having done something provocative to attract the attention of a thief. The irony emerging from the interplay of these two scenes then triggers a monologue directly to the audience on the absurdity and wrongness of blaming women for crimes against them. The second scene provides an interesting instance of how humour is used in street plays. In that particular scene, the comic effect works to not overwhelm the audience with the doubts about the guidelines themselves. It keeps the play engaging, as it serves to show the absurdity of blaming the woman victim in a situation of sexual harassment. Humour is often used as a really good way to point out certain things that ought to strike us as obvious, and like with the "marriage auction" and the priest in 'Om Swaha', humour also takes on a sort of sinister tone, because it points out a significant issue in a lighthearted way, even as the audience is aware that the issue at hand is not trivial at all. The scene in "Mahaul Badalna Hai" for example conveys important things about how we look at bodily autonomy, and forces the audience to look at the uncomfortable fact of how easily we choose to ignore the question of bodily autonomy and ownership of one's own sexuality in the case of harassment. Further, through the conversation amongst the characters, the play also tries to bring out the idea that consent has a very important role, as one does not want to take away the element of desire or playfulness in interactions between people. "Mahaul Badalna Hai" is a play that has been performed since the early 2000's, by various groups and different casts at various times. Many of us have played multiple characters in the play at different times, with floating cast, all replaceable, people just come in and perform. Over the years, the songs, the discussions and the interactions that are part of a street play have become a good way for people to get involved in the women's movement. Some people even end up getting attached to their characters, and it's very interesting to see Sahelis across generations connecting over their shared experiences of the play! The play and its songs were written entirely by Saheli members, its episodes derived from actual narratives from the report. Today, the songs have become part of a larger women's movement songbook itself, contributing to how street plays are enmeshed within the movement as a whole.  We also brought forth the point of change in reactions to the play from the audience over the years. In the early 2000's, the play was received with optimism that the proposed guidelines, the setting up of committees would lead to some advances in addressing sexual harassment at the workplace. However, audience discussions after play performances recently, in 2011-12 reveal a far greater cynicism with the workings of the law, especially as reports of threats, harassment and violence faced by women not only in their workplaces but other public spaces have become worryingly frequent. In such a milieu, in colleges especially, the talk has often turned into building solidarih'es with other women, through talking about their experiences and evolving strategies to help combat the everyday reality of sexual harassment. The two other plays that we discussed had been part of very different kinds of campaigns. The street play titled 'Norplant' was developed and performed in 1991-92, as part of a sustained campaign against hazardous contraceptives, in particular Norplant. Introduced as part of the then government's family planning programme in the 1990's, Norplant was an alternative long acting hormonal contraceptive 'implant' that was surgically inserted in women's bodies. The campaign against Norplant was well underway, with mass protests, demonstrations and activists crashing press conferences by the time the play came about. The campaign had an understanding of the connections that were being made between poverty and population explosion in the third world, which was driving a lot of the foreign funding behind contraceptive campaigns. Third world poor women became the easy targets of population control, and the play 'Norplant' came about with two main objectives - firstly to alert poor women, especially in urban bastis, to the trials and the contraceptive itself; and secondly to put pressure on the government to scrap the trials as they were hazardous and unethical. According to a Saheli who was part of creating and performing the play, "The decision of a street play seemed the fastest way to get to the lower middle class and basti women before they became targets." The play sought to highlight the coercive family planning programme, the politics of multinational corporations and the role of the health ministry, by satirising key players such as ministers and doctors, renaming the Health Minister, Mr Fotedaar as Khotedaar, (meaning unreliable), recreating scenes of how decision makers make hasty decisions, take action that serves their only own/global/funding/election purposes, or simply for meeting 'population targets'. It is these very actions that adversely impact poor women who are the subjects of their trials, who are given wrong information to get their consent, and are ultimately refused medical action in the end when they need it. The play was direct and satirical in its take on the Indian government, global governments and funding agencies. It was a well-travelled play that was performed in resettlement colonies and bastis all over the city, and always garnered a big audience of both men and women. The women in the audience were always responsive to the message, and shared their stories freely, leading to engaged discussions about reproductive health. Like 'Om Swaha', the cast included both men and women. While all the plays mentioned above were quite clearly campaign devices, the story of 'Kaun Jaat' has been slightly different. One of the major issues Saheli and several women's groups in the country have engaged with is the problem of growing communalism and the influence of right wing forces in the country. Post Gujarat genocide in 2002, many troubling questions about women's roles in situations of communal conflict arose. There was a need to look at connections between caste identity, religious identity and so on, and examine the various ways in which women are socialised into these and how they negotiate them in everyday life, particularly in the context of marriage and the family. A study conducted by Saheli in this context involved interviewing women in Delhi from varying backgrounds, about their lives in the context of their various identities of caste, class, religion and sexuality. When the report, titled 'Talking Marriage, Caste and Community - Voices From Within' was complete, many discussions and presentations followed. But we felt that a play would be a good way to clarify these interconnections, and trigger debates on how they impact and define women's lives. Hence, the play 'Kaun Jaat' (Literally, "What Caste?", but in common parlance, also used as "What regional, religious, linguistic and gender identity?"). Unlike the street play on sexual harassment, a script like Kaun Jaat would not primarily be a form of informationdissemination, but would rather be an awareness-raising exercise, an attempt to build connections between women's experiences and negotiations within the family, community and society. For us, Kaun Jaat became a way to articulate how women's differing locations in hierarchies shape the specificities of their oppressions, the challenges they face, and perhaps most importantly,to find ways to build bridges across these differences. This was a challenging play to write and perform, since it dealt with a range of issues and did not focus on a single problem or resolufi'on. After much conversafi'on and playing around with ideas, we decided to use monologues, derived in part from the interviews we had done for the report. What was important here was to bring out the interconnections between different forms of exploitative systems, in such a way that it could shake the audience. There were five monologues in all. The first character is a Dalit doctor, who talks about her experience of caste discrimination and the deep impact of the vicious anti-reservation movement in Delhi, especially within India's premium medical institution. Then there is a young Muslim woman who falls in love and marries a Hindu and abides by his family's condition to convert and subsume her own religious identity - her loneliness and pain is telling. The third is a woman who, years after being in a traditional arranged marriage who realises she is not quite 'happily married' like she was deluding herself. Then, a photographer talks about coming out as a lesbian to her family, even as she discusses the difficulty of working things out with her partner. The play's last monologue talks about sexual violence in situations of conflict - between communities and even with the State - and brings out the connections between different kinds of violence and oppressions, and how women's bodies are frequently the sites of violence. The monologues are interspersed with powerful poetry and satirical songs that show the absurdity of rigid religious and community norms that control women's lives. The subtlety and irony with which Kaun Jaat plays, within the more direct parameters of a street play, has been received very differently in different contexts. While most audiences respond knowingly to the questions being raised, there have been some memorable instances where it has come across as reinforcing hierarchies, leading to audience members questioning the play and its message itself. All in all, Kaun Jaat has led to some very thoughtful and interesting discussions. At the end of the presentation we once again raised the question as to why is it important for us to talk about street plays as a text for the women's movement. Street plays, both with their content and form, are important devices of individual campaigns or larger social questions that the women's movement seeks to undertake as we have seen above. The journey of a street play, from its conception to its writing to its performance, its discussions and its after life, can serve as an illustration of the life of the campaign and shed light on some facets of politics of the movement as a whole. In themselves, street plays are an important way of doing politics for the women's movement as well, in simple physical terms of gathering an audience that is mostly dominated by women, claiming a public space and turning it into a place of discussion and debate, and a creative way of reaching out to people, spreading awareness or raising concerns about issues. Street plays can thus provide us with an alternative history of the movement, embedded in the stories, reminiscences, discussions and songs that are associated with each play.The history of plays in a collective like Saheli is also one of reviving feminist energies, with new women joining in for the play performance but staying on for just about everything, and a language of protest and struggle embodied in songs and dialogues that link us across generations and groups.

subtitle: A Learning Experience
contentEn: Saheli teaching a women's studies course? Saheli of the rallies and protests? Believe it or not - yes! More than two years ago, the curriculum for the post-graduate Women's Studies Course for the Mahatma Gandhi International Hindi University was evolving and a core group responsible for this invited Saheli to be a part of the discussion. It came as a pleasant surprise that besides calling hard-core academicians, women from an activist group were also invited to be a part of the process. So one of us decided to explore what exactly it was all about. That was the beginning of our involvement in these discussions and unfolding of an educating experience. A Journey Into The Unknown Teaching an academic course was a novel experience. During the discussions about the scope of the subjects, the complexity which should be achieved, the format of the course and so on, we were slightly out of our depth. After agreeing upon the curriculum, various people were taking responsibilities of designing syllabus for papers to be taught over a two-year period. We had vehemently stated that women's health is an area which should be covered in some detail in this curriculum, and lo and behold, the responsibility of designing the syllabus for a paper landed on our shoulders. That is when we started getting a bit worried about what we were in for! The Indian Association of Women's Studies (IAWS) has always talked about getting academicians and activists together to discuss issues. In biannual conferences of IAWS this mix of academics and activists is visible. Here also with our work as women's health activists central to our understanding, we tried to achieve a balance in the syllabus between the theoretical understanding of women's health and the role of women's movements in striving for better health status for all women. With our diverse backgrounds and varied professional lives we managed to come up with a syllabus for a paper in the M.A. degree course.  While many teachers associated with the women's studies course all over the country are extremely competent, very few of them specialise in women's health. In fact, very few centres offer health as a special subject. Even while working as women's health activists our experience is that many activists in the women's movement find health a difficult subject to engage with. Like a handful of other women's groups across the country, Saheli has a tradition of working on many health-related issues over the past 20-odd years. To translate our hands-on experiences of fighting legal cases, campaigns, surveys, exhibitions, demonstrations and sit-ins on women's health issues and present them in an academic format was as challenging as it was exciting. Evolving Teaching Methods In early 2004 we conducted a workshop in the Saheli office for students from the course who had come from Wardha to Delhi on a study tour. We met the enthusiastic bunch of students for the first time, and to our pleasant surprise, both men and women had enrolled for the course. The young men told us of the opposition they had to face from their families, who felt that a women's studies course was a worthless qualification for a young man! For the women, most of them from conservative backgrounds, doing a post-graduation and staying in a hostel involved challenging the norms within their families.  This workshop was more an out-of-the-classroom experience. It did not talk about the methodology of teaching, or history of the subject but it straight away gave the students an essence of what campaigns on women's health have been all about. How demands made on the basis of information and studies can be translated into public activity and protests, whether these work as strategies to achieve the goals, what different forms of protests can be used in such situations and so on. As the flyover shook and window panes rattled, we tried to share our practical work experiences without too much pontification. Answering piercing questions, and formulating answers to complex queries helped us sharpen our own understanding. We also gave the students an assignment to produce a newsletter on the "population problem". And the wonderfully produced assignment we graded six months later were proof that they had found the session as stimulating as we had! Onwards To Wardha From late 2004, the co-ordinator of the course, Uma Chakravarti began to persuade us to go to Wardha to teach all or part of the whole paper we had designed earlier. In a way, this was extremely positive feedback for our syllabus, since "Women and Health", from being an optional course had been "promoted" to a compulsory course, apparently because the syllabus effectively laid out how an understanding of the politics of women's health could provide an understanding of other linkages that impact on women's lives. But admittedly, our collective hearts sank at the onerous responsibility. This was not something we could do easily, as the expertise required for designing a syllabus is different from actually teaching the entire course. Ultimately, we agreed and decided to teach a part of the syllabus we had designed. Experts, academicians and activists from other parts of the country filled in and competently handled the rest of the teaching responsibility. Some of us reached Wardha earlier in the year with much anxiety and trepidation. Part of it was to do with teaching in Hindi, part of it was to do with classroom teaching as a form of instruction which we were expected to adopt in the environs of the University unlike in our office in Delhi! Despite delays and disorganisation resulting in our reaching later than planned, a warm welcome from the students and their willingness to continue classes after formal office hours won our hearts and dissipated the anxiety. In classrooms and in the shade of huge trees, we plunged into teaching- which consisted of raising issues and concerns, providing part of the information, asking students to get more information on the subject, evaluating their ability to synthesise information and come up with answers in response to exercises and helping them in becoming questioning, critical and analytical individuals.  Four of the Sahelis were involved in this teaching experience at different points during the course of two years, it was a unique experience for us for a variety of reasons. Firstly, we were proud of being a part of the group framing a curriculum for the first ever masters level programme in Women's Studies in Hindi. Secondly, for some of us teaching a formal course in a university and giving it just enough tilt so that it does not remain only an academic course taught within the confines of a classroom was a new and enjoyable process. Finally, it was also an experience worth cherishing because it was rewarding to see the faces lighting up as the penny dropped as we moved from one argument to the other in the close interactions. The same students came back the next day and asked for more information, and argued with us. The informal nature of the teaching was more conducive to dialogue and exchange of ideas than having a monologue in the classroom full of students. We think this experience has enriched us as much as it probably has the students of the course! The fact of the Women's Studies Course at the MG! Hindi University hangs in a balance due to administrative problems. If it were indeed to close down, and the experiment crushed before it has time to blossom, it would be a pity, and a loss to women's studies in India.

subtitle: An Announcement
An appeal for support
contentEn: Saheli was set up by a small group of women in 1981 as a resource centre, primarily for providing support and alternatives for women in crisis situations. Over the years, we became increasingly involved in campaigns against domestic violence, dowry, rape, sexual harassment, police atrocities on women and discrimination against women in the law. Simultaneously, we also began work on issues related to women's health and their representation in the media, and campaigned against sex determination tests, dangerous drugs and hazardous contraceptives being introduced in the country. In 1991, we closed our crisis centre and decided to strengthen campaign work. As a small group, we felt that our energies were better spent in areas where other groups are not active. Today, we continue our campaign against hazardous contraceptives and coercive population control. We are also working towards evolving an egalitarian civil code for all. In order to make our campaigns broadbased we are joining hands with other groups. We also actively support local initiatives in other parts of the country: campaigns against communalism and highlighting the issue of violence against women. Through our work we hope to build courage and conviction that would enable women to come together to create a just society where we can all live with hope and dignity. Our Financial Situation When Saheli was started, friends and sympathisers helped us with funds as and when we needed them. In fact, we have always relied on individual contributions as opposed to governmental or institutional funds. We feel that this allows us to maintain our autonomy while at the same time, keeping us responsible towards people like you who share our concerns and offer us support in our ideas and work. With an increase in our campaign work, coordination with other groups and our efforts to take the issue to wider sections we feel an urgent need for a steady flow of contributions. For the coming year, we need Rs. 10,000 to 15,000 a month for campaign material, travel and administrative expenses, telephone and electricity bills, publications etc. In order to more efficiently coordinate all that we have on hand today, we wish to keep the option of working as fulltimers open. In the past, your help has made it possible for us to raise the funds we have needed. Today, we believe that your support can make it possible once again. We would be able to meet our requirements if even 200–300 individuals could contribute Rs. 50 per month. We value every contribution, however big or small. Our Activities Cheques and drafts should be made out to SAHELI. Please specify whether you will contribute on a monthly/quarterly/annual basis.

subtitle: An Update
contentEn: In an earlier edition of the Newsletter (May 1988), we gave a report on 'Child Murder: Police Inaction Continues'. This is to update our readers on the situation in Anand Parbat. Initially, many efforts were made to persuade the authorities that some action was needed against the SHO of the Anand Parbat Police Station, but our letters to the Lt. Governor, the Commissioner of Police, the Crimes against Women Cell and various other departments of the police, went unheeded. It almost seemed as if the culprit of the case was being given total protection. We had heard that the SHO has been suspended but he was sighted at a post in Palam Airport - as for the reports that he had been arrested, these were a little difficult to believe, because Kamlesh came with accounts of how the man had been seen by her in Anand Parbat on more than one occasion. Meanwhile, volunteers had checked up in the hospital where Naresh had been admitted, and the existence of 'Medical Records' was confirmed. We visited the hospital and were assured that such a file indeed existed, but it was a 'Top Security' file and we were not permitted to examine it. Armed with this information, we consulted our lawyers, and on their advice, a public interest Litigation was filed in the Supreme Court before the vacation judge, who admitted the case and issued an order that the medical records be placed under seal in the Supreme Court. As soon as the Supreme Court reopened after the vacation, Kamlesh's case was heard and immediate steps were taken to ensure that: - Even though these orders were clearly passed by the Court, it took a long time for them to be implemented. Mean- time, Kamlesh was attending hearings regularly. Alongside these hearings, a police investigation was started - a type of cross examination of Kamlesh's evidence was carried out. During these, a volunteer from Saheli was always present. Maya Devi was given back the tenancy of her room in October 1988. The electricity and water supply has very recently been reconnected (Dec.1988) but the summons for Kamlesh to appear in the lower court did not stop. Nor has the police harassment stopped. Right till now she is visited at her home by members of the police force, and various summons are being served on her. The criminal cases against the SHO are also going on simultaneously in the lower court. Meanwhile, we have asked that Kamlesh should get complete compensation for the great loss she has had in Naresh's untimely death, and the indignities she has suffered on her person, and also for the life of fear she has been leading since November 1987. Note: The co-petitioners in the case filed in November 87 were Action India, Ankur, Shakti Shalini, Mrinal Pande (individual) and others.

subtitle: Police Inaction Continues
contentEn: Naresh, the 9-year-old son of Kamlesh, died on the 26th of November 1987 as a result of physical violence instigated by the police. Kamlesh lives in a tiny, ill-lit single room in Delhi's Anand Parbat, a lower middle class colony. The room, along with many similar rooms which sur- round an open courtyard, and which have a single main entrance, is presently being disputed in court. Anand Parbat, a colony which developed irregularly after Partition, has now become a very lucrative area for property developers, as it lies adjacent to large commercial and industrial areas. As a lot of money is involved, the local police, including the SHO Lal Singh, are involved in numerous illegal land deals. As Kamlesh's husband is a long-haul truck driver Kamlesh stays alone in the room with her children, all minors. Kamlesh's actual landlord, who became missing during the November 1984 riots in Delhi, could not prove his ownership, and Kamlesh obtained a stay order from the court against eviction. Meanwhile, two men, claiming to be the new landlords, evicted the other residents of the building with the help of the local police. The SHO, Lal Singh, kept harassing Kamlesh -- at times offering her Rs. 10,000 to leave the place, and at other times calling her unnecessarily to the police station and verbally abusing her. On the 13th of November, when Kamleshi was out, Lal Singh arrested her three children and kept them without food and water in the lock up the whole day. Ultimately, Kamlesh's lawyer's intervention was needed to get the children back. On the evening of the 14th, Lal Singh (in mufti), with some other police and the two so-called landlords entered Kamlesh's room at 7.30 pm. and accused her of trespassing. Kamlesh was alone with her son Naresh. He started abusing and threatening her, and Naresh clung to her legs. Lal Singh then ordered the rest of the men in the room to kill the child to teach the mother a lesson, pulled the boy and flung him across the room, where the two landlords hit him repeatedly with bricks. The police then dragged Kamlesh to the police station where they tore her clothes, and beat her some more. Lal Singh then took her to the Paharganj police station, where Kamlesh became unconscious. The police advised him to have an MLC done for her, but instead he brought her back to Anand Parbat, put her in the lock up, from where she was taken to Tihar Jail and then released two days later. In the meantime, Kamlesh's children were taken in by a neighbour. When Kamlesh returned home, her son was seriously ill and local doctors advised hospitalization. Naresh was finally admitted into the Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, where no MIC was automatically done, as the police there insisted that Lal Singh, when contacted, claimed there was no case for an MIC. Shortly Naresh went into a coma, from which he did not recover. Kamlesh and her lawyer approached several police personnel, to have an MLC done for Naresh and to register a case against Lal Singh, Shambu Dayal and the others, but to no avail. Finally, on the 23rd, the ACP of Patel Nagar, within whose area Anand Parbat falls, agreed to come the next day, as he claimed to be extremely busy with VIP security that day. He however did find the time to go to the local doctors of Anand Parbat and to the neighbour who had taken in the children, and got statements from them that the injuries were not due to beating, and were more recent than the 14th. In the FIR which he made out for Kamlesh, he added the statement "the police did not beat my son. Shambu Dayal and his son were arrested on charges of attempted murder. A late MLC was carried out on the 24th when Naresh was in a coma, which clearly underlined the injuries. However, the post mortem report, carried out at the police hospital, mentioned the cause of death as pneumonitis, and stated that the injuries had nothing to do with the death. Later when we spoke to some of the doctors who had attended to the child, we were told that pneumonitis was due to the injuries, and so the death of the child was clearly related to the beating. Kamlesh, her husband, lawyer and some neigh- bours approached the Lt. Governor of Delhi for justice. After offering to transfer Lal Singh as a sop, the Lt. Governor instituted an SDM (Sub-divisional Magistrate) enquiry into the matter. On the 5th of December, the vigilance branch of the Delhi police made out a confidential report where Lal Singh was implicated in the death, and where they clearly stated that the accused should not be released on bail as this would hinder the enquiry. Lal Singh was sent on leave, but returned before the enquiry was over. The charges against Shambu Dayal and his son were changed and they were released on bail, The SDM in charge of the enquiry who was very willing to listen to various witnesses, suddenly overnight became extre- mely secretive and refused to share his findings. Since then, Shambu Dayal has cut off the electricity and water connections of Kamlesh's room: the latrine has been broken, and Kamlesh continues to be abused and threatened at all hours of the day and night. Lal Singh, who already has cases of assault and bribe against him at the Delhi High Court and who is out on bail at present, refuses to register any complaints made by Kamlesh, instead he has terrorized the neighbours and has forced them to file complaints against her. Saheli took up Kamlesh's case and organized a meeting of various women's and civil rights groups. Together they demanded from the Lt. Governor that Lal Singh, Shambu Dayal and his son be arrested and that the findings of the SDM inquiry be made public. No action has been taken so far. The Commissioner of Police, Delhi, when contacted, has repeatedly adopted delaying tactics by suggesting that we get to the Crimes Against Women Cell, and from there to various departments none of whom is ready to say or do anything positive. Meanwhile Kamlesh continues to survive in this oppressive atmosphere, terrified of what may happen to her and her surviving children any time. Kamlesh's case is yet another proof of women's extreme vulnerability in the face of police atrocities. Reports pouring in from all over the country of rapes by police only confirm this, and faced with the complicity within all levels of police and other law enforcement machinery, we are left with no choice but so take law into our own hands.

Shanta came to us a few months ago; she was referred to Saheli by another organization. When Shanta walked in at the door, she looked like an abject sight-- dishevelled, distraught and when she started talking, she was never far from tears. Shanta Story: "I was married in 1978-I saw Madan and Madan saw me; we fell in love and in spite of strong opposition from our families, we were married-we are from different communities, you see, so the elders were very strongly against our marriage- "Eventually, when we started our household, every- thing was perfect. Our first child, a daughter, was born in 1980. Our second daughter came in 1982, and our son in 1985. Outwardly we gave the impression of a happy family-but this was only a facade, because an insidious rot had set in, which was gnawing at the very foundations of our lives. "My husband, apparently, was not satisfied with what he had-a wife, three children and an income of Rs. 10,000/- per month. So he started looking for fresh amusements until he found his entertainment in a series of other women. He began taunting me on my inability to produce more sons--You have two daughters and one son-you are incapable of bearing male children". ...only one son? My friends have all sons and you have produced only one' were taunts that filled my ears, and finally, he turned his taunts and threats into actualities, and the ever-changing series of women friends he would bring over to my house, and entertain increased. "Ultimately, the 'other' women were occupying my bed and home and I was subjected to all manner of physical abuse. He kept telling me that I should bring more and more 'gifts' from my parents and then he might and then he might consider mending his ways. My parents are old and not well off, I could not comply with his increasing demands, so the harassment grew and grew until I could stand it no more. I poured myself a glassful of Baygon spray and drank it.  "I woke up in the hospital. I had been rushed there by a badly frightened husband, who thought he would be arrested if I died in the house. No one from my house came to visit me--my two daughters had been told that I was dead. When I recovered I went to my parent's home. "I was shattered-on the brink of breakdown, but my parents and my friends rallied and I realized that life was still worth fighting for. "Today, I am quite a different woman-my friends and family find it hard to see the broken Shanta they knew and I have found a new meaning to life. Today, I have my two daughters with me and I am negotiating to get my son also. "Meantime, the main thing I have learnt is that when I want to, I can do anything; I do have the strength and I will live my life in peace. If my husband cares to join me in this, I will be happy, I have the ability to get what-ever I want, for myself." Shanta today is a completely changed woman, she came to visit the other day, I could hardly recognize her -she walked, with an air of competence. She was on her way to take custody of her two daughters from the police station. I was worried- would she manage? "Shall I come with you? Are you all right ?" I asked. Back come the answer - "I will go and see what happens. I think I can manage; if I need help, I will telephone you". Today she is living with her parents, has found herself a job, and seems to be in full charge of the situation, because that telephone call for help has yet to come. Shanta is one of the women who did not really want to take the path of least resistance, and do away with herself rather than find alternatives. She realized that she had more to lose-so she rallied to the medications given in the hospital. Once out from there, she had the whole-hearted support of her parents who took her home and nursed her in an atmosphere of love and safety. Apart from the support she has had from family, friends and institutions, Shanta drew on her own renewed store of strength, to fight for her rights as a woman, and today is able to go about what she needs to do for herself, by herself, secure in the knowledge that she can do whatever she wants, and that help over the rougher patches, is hers for the asking.

subtitle: An Open Letter to the Minister

contentEn: Saheli was set up six years ago in 1981, by a small group of women. Our experiences with anti-dowry campaigns and issues related to rape, women's health and legal rights, through the seventies, made us aware of the urgent need to provide space and opportunity to individual women to rebuild their lives. The brutality and violence against women prevalent in our society, deprive women of the right to live with dignity and self-respect. Changing patterns of family, clash of values, compounded by economic pressures have made women victims of growing mental and physical torture. Saheli Women's Resource Centre is a place women come to, to find the means to live a dignified life. Over 500 women have come to us in the last six years, seeking help. Our attempt is to share our experiences, and collectively seek solutions to our problems. A woman's desire to confront her situation and assert herself, is half the battle. We give courage to every woman struggling to emerge from the crisis in her life, to stand on her own, in the knowledge that she is not alone. Providing support to individual women takes up a substantial portion of our time. In addition, in the coming year we intend to do the following: With these activities we hope to reach out to women in the neighbouring slums, to university students, working women and housewives, and hope to raise their awareness. When we started, we had no money. With donations of Rs. 80/- and contributions from friends, and volunteers giving their time, we struggled to keep Saheli open six days a week. We functioned from a garage donated by a volunteer. Since then we have grown, and so have our needs for funds. While a number of us are contributing our time and money for Saheli work, we still need money for our office and five full time workers. Since the beginning, we have relied on individual support rather than institutional, foreign and governmental funds for carrying out our activities. This we feel helps us remain responsible to all who contribute their resources. It also helps us to remain independent of various pressures on our values which are invariably exerted by institutional donors, including that of making us complacent. For the coming year, we need Rs. 10,000/- a month to pay office rent, support five full time workers and to meet administrative and other expenses. We need your financial support for this cause. We value every rupee you give with sympathy and concern. Contributions to Saheli are eligible for exemption u/s 80G of the Income Tax Act, 1961. Saheli Women’s Resource Centre Office above shop 105–108 Under Defence Colony Flyover New Delhi – 110024 Phone: 616485

titleEn: Women Home Workers in the Garment Industry

contentEn: I am 32 years old. I was born in a small village in Rampur zilla of Uttar Pradesh. We were eleven brothers and sisters, that is what my mother said. Only three of us survived. One brother, one sister and I. When I was seventeen my elder sister drowned herself in a well. Her mother-in-law used to beat her and abuse her constantly. She was given more work than she could possibly do. In desperation she killed herself, leaving behind one daughter and one son. When was I married? I don't remember. Possibly when I was twelve or thirteen years old. After six years I went to live with my husband. He was a Kisan. He leased land and we earned enough to live on. My mother had given me a buffalo which I took care of. I milked it, fed it, cleaned it and sold ghee and butter. I also kept some chicken. At the end of the week I always had some money. My husband always took this away. Morning, noon, and night I worked. My mother died, so I also took care of my brother's house. I looked after 4 of our animals and six of his, cutting grass, cleaning both the houses and cooking. I cannot give you an account of the work I have done in my life. It is too much. My husband was always quarreling with me. He did not love me or the children. When my son was sick, I had to take him to the doctor. Once, I was also unwell. The child and I were both vomiting, but he did not accompany us. Somehow, I managed to save my son, though he had money he refused to give it, I had to walk miles to get to the doctor. He only loved his money. He harassed me constantly, threatening to sell my buffalo every week at the local market. I somehow begged and persuaded him not to. Twice he also beat me and I resolved that I could not live with such indignity. Though I loved my brother very much and did all his work in the house, he also did not care for me. For very small things, he would also beat me and I felt I could not go to his house for help. For many weeks I cried every day and wondered whether I should kill myself. Then I worried about what would happen to my children. I decided to go away with my children after Ramzan. Now it is six years since I left home and three years since I came to Delhi. A family I knew for twenty years helped me to get a job in Allahabad. But they also cheated me. I kept 3 tolas of gold and nine hundred rupees in their custody. After one year when I asked for it, they avoided talking about it and then said they cannot give it back because they had used it up for their son's marriage. What could I do? In Allahabad I worked in a house for Rs. twenty a month. I used to work from 4 a.m. in the morning till midnight everyday with- out holidays and could not save any money. My daughter meanwhile was working with a family in Delhi and I decided to also come and work in Delhi. Finding work was not easy. I walked for miles in Nizamuddin looking for work. People turned me out saying "there is no work here". An old couple gave me shelter in their Jhuggi and as soon as I got work, I rented a house. I was forced to change maliks many times because they would give too much work and too little money. One malik accused me of theft when I went to ask for my wages and locked me in his house. I somehow escaped and went to lodge a police complaint. I came to know that this man behaved badly with all his servants. One day the jamadarni told me I should go to the Saheli office and they would help me to find work, I did not find more work, but I have become a part of Saheli. I have been helped and I also give help to other women. We meet in the basti once a week and discuss our problems, about work, husbands, children and many other things. For the last few months my room has also been used as a shelter. Women from the age of sixteen to forty-five along with them. Children have shared my house. I feel we women have to help each other. “Sakina people say women can't live alone, they need a man, protection, don’t you have problems?" I feel a single woman can live comfortably if she is willing to work hard. I live with both my child- ren and am educating them. I have always worked in the village, in my mother's house, in my husband's house and now. People respect me because I work and earn my living and do not do any wrong things. Sometimes men have tried to make suggestions, but I clearly tell them that I believe in work and do not want any favours. I ask all women, what is the use of going from one man to another? Is our life only in the hands of men? Can't we think, don't we work hard? I feel people will respect us if we learn to be independent and respect ourselves.
